source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Phosphorus (P) is described as one of the two most commonly limiting nutrients for corn in Cambodia (along with nitrogen), because most native soils tested low in available P. Phosphorus deficiency shows up as purple or reddish discoloration on leaves, especially on lower/older leaves, and is often more visible under cool conditions.

DAP (di-ammonium phosphate, 18% N, 20% P, 1.6% S) is the most common phosphorus source. Research from Vietnam, the Philippines, and Australia on acidic upland red soils (Blamey et al. 2002) found that phosphorus fertilizer is most effective when banded below the seed row at planting, at a rate equivalent to roughly 26-39 kg P/ha. Applying DAP at 100 kg/ha supplies about 20 kg P/ha -- applying it at planting time, banded near the seed, is described as the most effective method; regardless of method, deep placement of phosphorus has limited benefit because corn's early root system stays relatively shallow.

Corn's association with naturally occurring mycorrhizal fungi can improve phosphorus uptake in low-P soils, but this beneficial fungal relationship can be reduced by soil disturbance (tillage) and by heavy chemical fertilizer use -- worth bearing in mind when planning both tillage and fertilizer programs together.
